title: Shabbat morning
hook: in a synagogue, a park, or at home with the portion
tomorrow: two schools argue over one word in the Havdalah blessing. which?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the nap: even God, says Exodus, rested and was refreshed. Rest is holy. Now you're awake, it's Shabbat morning, and the week's portion is waiting.

Before answering a long, tricky message, plenty of people read it twice: once for what it says, once for what it means. The Talmud asks something like that of the weekly Torah portion, with a twist. Read it twice in the original, it says, and then once more, in a translation. That's the puzzle. Why read the same verses twice, and why a third time in another language?
screen: `READ IT TWICE BEFORE REPLYING.` → `TWICE THE VERSE.` → `ONCE THE TRANSLATION.` → `WHY?`

segments.voice: The rule is in the Talmud's tractate Berakhot: a person should complete their portions along with the community, the scripture twice and the targum once. The Targum is the old Aramaic translation, the one ordinary people once understood. The Talmud even attaches a promise: whoever completes the portions with the community has their days and years lengthened. So, the puzzle. The text doesn't explain the numbers, so readers have offered answers. One: the first reading is for the words, the second is for hearing yourself in them. Another: a text only pronounced isn't yet a text understood, and the translation is the way in. Later law codes allowed a commentary like Rashi's to stand in for the Targum, which tells you what the third reading is for: understanding. It's an old instinct. In Nehemiah, when Ezra reads the Torah to the gathered people, the readers give the sense, so that everyone understands what they hear. And notice the phrase, with the community. Every week, Jews in many places read the same portion. In a synagogue, it's read aloud from the scroll. In a park, from a printed book on a bench. At home, at the kitchen table before anyone's up. The place can change. What stays is the portion, and that you read it in step with everyone else reading it that week. One to tell a friend tonight: the Talmud's rule builds a translation right into the reading.
screen: `TWICE THE VERSE, ONCE THE TARGUM.` · `TO HEAR IT, THEN TO UNDERSTAND.` · `A SCROLL, A BENCH, A KITCHEN.` · `IN STEP WITH THE COMMUNITY.` · then, large: `MORNING OF THE PORTION.`

segments.voice: Find this week's portion, or any short passage of Torah you have on hand. Read one verse twice, slowly, then say it once in your own plain words. Write that plain version by hand, one line: your own small targum.
screen: `ONE VERSE, TWICE.` · `ONCE IN YOUR OWN WORDS.` · `WRITE YOUR TARGUM.`

Targum.meaning: the old Aramaic translation of the Torah

Aramaic.meaning: a sister language of Hebrew, used in the Talmud

Berakhot.meaning: the Talmud tractate on blessings and prayer

Rashi.meaning: a medieval commentator on the Torah and Talmud

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 8a-b (complete the portions with the community, scripture twice and Targum once; days and years lengthened)
Shulchan Aruch, Orach Chaim 285 (reading the portion; Rashi's commentary may serve in place of the Targum)
Nehemiah 8:8 (they read in the book distinctly, gave the sense, and caused them to understand)

notes: Berakhot 8a-b: 'a person should always complete his portions with the community, twice scripture and once targum', with the promise of lengthened days and years; paraphrased. Confirm.
The two explanations of 'why twice' are offered as what readers have suggested; the Talmud gives no reason. Confirm the framing.
Shulchan Aruch OC 285:2 on Rashi in place of the Targum; confirm the section.
Nehemiah 8:8 paraphrased (the readers gave the sense so the people understood); the Talmud (Megillah 3a) reads part of this verse as the Targum, not stated in the voice. Confirm.
'Every week, Jews in many places read the same portion' avoids claiming everyone does (Israel and the diaspora sometimes differ by a week). Confirm.
